more: On the early sea floor, warm, hydrogen-rich water seeped out of rock chimneys riddled with tiny pores. That fluid was alkaline, while the ocean outside was more acidic, and only a thin mineral wall separated the two. The difference worked like a battery, pushing charged particles across the wall, much as every living cell still makes its energy today. Many scientists think this free power started life's chemistry, though the idea is still debated. The Lost City vent field in the Atlantic has chimneys up to 60 meters tall.
link3_title: Life in the extreme: hydrothermal vents

more: The first protocells could not see, hear or search for anything. They reacted only when a molecule happened to drift up to their mineral or fatty walls and stick. Sensing and acting were one event: the molecule touched, a reaction ran, and that was all. This is the simplest possible answer to what a system can sense, and every later sense improved on it. Even today, a bacterium's senses begin with a molecule bumping into a protein on its surface.

Before nerves, the only way a signal could travel was diffusion: molecules jiggling at random until they happen to arrive. The catch is that the time grows with the square of the distance, so going 10 times farther takes 100 times longer. A small molecule crosses 1 micrometer, about the width of a bacterium, in roughly half a millisecond. Crossing 1 millimeter takes about 8 minutes. That is fast enough inside one cell but hopeless for a large body, which is why animals later evolved nerves.

Self-feeding chemistry is a set of reactions whose products help make more of the same products, so the system speeds itself up. In the vent pores, hydrogen and carbon dioxide could react on iron-sulfur minerals to build small carbon molecules, a process called carbon fixation. Some of those molecules then helped the next round of reactions along. This loop was the planet's first processor: chemistry that turns inputs into outputs by fixed rules. Some microbes still fix carbon this way, using iron-sulfur proteins.

A protocell's only working memory was how much of each chemical it held at that moment. If one molecule was plentiful and another scarce, that pattern was a kind of state, like a row of switches set on or off. All together this came to roughly 100 bits, or about 100 yes-or-no answers held at once. The state faded fast, because molecules leaked away or reacted, so nothing was held for long. Later cells learned to make such chemical levels last on purpose.

Once some molecules could help make copies of themselves, a new rule took over: whatever copied fastest and most accurately became more common. Copies were never perfect, so small changes appeared, and the better copiers outgrew the rest. This is natural selection working on chemistry, before anything was truly alive. In the lab, scientists have built pairs of RNA molecules that copy each other, and in 2024 researchers led by Blaise Agüera y Arcas showed that even tiny random computer programs bumping into each other with no goal spontaneously form self-copying code.

RNA is a chain molecule that can carry information in its sequence of letters and also fold into shapes that speed up reactions. RNA molecules that act like enzymes are called ribozymes. Many scientists think early life ran on RNA before DNA and proteins existed, an idea called the RNA world. Mineral surfaces such as clay may have helped build these chains and protect them. Storage was tiny: the whole planet may have held only about 20,000 unique bits, less than a short text file.

A single vent chimney is riddled with thousands of tiny compartments, many smaller than a millimeter, linked by cracks and channels. All of them draw on the same flow of warm fluid, so they share one power supply. Molecules made in one pore can drift into its neighbors, so useful chemicals spread through the cluster. This made the first network: many separate reaction chambers behaving a little like one larger system. Real chimneys, such as those at the Lost City vent field, are full of such pores.

The ribosome is a molecular machine that reads a gene's message and builds a protein from it. It moves along a strand of messenger RNA three letters at a time, and each three-letter word, called a codon, calls for one amino acid. Its working core is made of RNA, a leftover from the RNA world. A bacterial ribosome adds about 15 to 20 amino acids per second, so a typical 300-amino-acid protein takes under half a minute. Proteins became life's tools for sensing, moving and computing.
link2_title: Translation: DNA to mRNA to protein

more: The genetic code is the lookup table that turns three-letter codons into amino acids. There are 64 possible codons for 20 amino acids plus stop signals, so most amino acids have several codons, which makes many copying typos harmless. Nearly all life uses the same table, with only small variations, which is strong evidence that all living things share one ancestor. A shared code also means a gene from one cell can work in another. Proofreading steps catch most mistakes as the code is read.
link2_title: The information in DNA determines cellular function via translation

more: DNA is a double-stranded molecule that stores genes more safely than RNA, because each strand backs up the other. Nine years before DNA's double helix was found in 1953, physicist Erwin Schrödinger predicted in What Is Life? that genes had to be an 'aperiodic crystal': a stable molecule whose non-repeating chain of letters acts as a code. One 2024 study dated the last universal common ancestor, or LUCA, to about 4.2 billion years ago with roughly 2.5 million DNA letters, while other studies give smaller gene sets. Modern bacteria copy DNA with about one mistake per billion letters.
link2_title: LUCA: the last universal common ancestor

more: Microbes do not only pass genes down to their offspring. They also hand them sideways to neighbors, by trading small rings of DNA, picking up DNA left by dead cells, or having viruses carry genes across. In crowded microbial mats, a useful trick, like digesting a new food, could spread through many species quickly. This turned the mat into a shared library of genes rather than a set of separate cells. The oldest fossil mats are about 3.5 billion years old, but gene swapping itself is thought to be older still. Today the same process spreads antibiotic resistance between bacteria.
link2_title: Microbial mats offer clues to life on early Earth

more: Early photosynthesis captured sunlight but did not split water, so it released no oxygen. Instead, bacteria took electrons from hydrogen sulfide, hydrogen or dissolved iron, which were plentiful in the early ocean. Purple and green sulfur bacteria still work this way today, leaving behind sulfur instead of oxygen. Sunlight is a vastly bigger power source than vent chemistry, so life could spread across the sunlit surface of the sea. That extra energy fed more cells and whole communities of partners.
link2_title: Microbial mats offer clues to life on early Earth

more: Bacteria such as E. coli carry clusters of receptor proteins that grab food molecules like sugars and amino acids. To move, they spin flagella, thin whips each turned by a tiny rotary motor built into the cell's surface. Spinning one way, the flagella bundle together and push the cell straight; reversing makes it tumble and point in a new random direction. Now sensing connects to action, because what the receptors detect changes how the motors turn. E. coli swims about 20 to 30 micrometers per second.
link2_title: Bacterial chemotaxis: to tumble or not to tumble?

more: To tell whether food is getting closer, a bacterium must compare now with a moment ago. E. coli does this with chemical tags called methyl groups that are slowly added to or removed from its receptors. The tags lag a few seconds behind the food level, so the gap tells the cell whether things are improving. This working memory lasts about 4 seconds and is held in chemistry, not nerves. It lets a cell 2 micrometers long notice changes too small to measure across its own body.
link2_title: Bacterial chemotaxis: to tumble or not to tumble?

more: Bacteria cannot steer, yet they still find food with one simple rule. A cell swims straight for about a second, then tumbles to face a random new direction. If its short memory says food is increasing, it waits longer before tumbling, so good directions last longer and bad ones get cut short. Over many runs this bias adds up, and the cell drifts toward the food. It is the planet's first program that uses the recent past to choose the next action.
link2_title: Bacterial chemotaxis: to tumble or not to tumble?

more: Syntrophy means feeding together: one microbe's waste becomes another microbe's meal. For example, some bacteria break down food and release hydrogen, which would soon stall their own chemistry if it built up. Methane-making microbes nearby eat that hydrogen and keep their partners working. Neither could live as well alone. In What Is Life? and What Is Intelligence?, Blaise Agüera y Arcas points to such metabolic partnerships as early symbiogenesis: evolution advancing by cooperation, not competition alone.
link2_title: Microbial mats offer clues to life on early Earth

more: Cyanobacteria learned to use sunlight to split water and released oxygen as waste. Water is everywhere, so life no longer depended on scarce supplies of hydrogen sulfide or iron. Scientists still debate when this began; chemical clues show whiffs of oxygen before 2.5 billion years ago, and many think the process is older. Oxygen built up slowly until, around 2.4 billion years ago, it began filling the air in the Great Oxidation Event. That oxygen later became a powerful fuel for breathing.
link3_title: Whiffs and the rise of oxygen

more: Cyanobacteria live on sunlight, so it pays to get ready before dawn instead of reacting after it. They keep time with just three proteins, called KaiA, KaiB and KaiC. KaiC slowly adds and then removes phosphate tags, and one full cycle takes about 24 hours. Mixed in a test tube with ATP, the cell's energy molecule, the three proteins keep ticking for days. With this clock, life could plan hours ahead instead of seconds.

In quorum sensing, every cell releases a small signal molecule and also listens for it. When few cells are around the signal stays faint, but when many crowd together it rises past a threshold and they all switch behavior at once. This lets a group act only when it is big enough to succeed, a bit like a vote. The bacterium Vibrio fischeri glows only when packed densely inside a squid's light organ. Mats of billions of cells could coordinate the same way.
link2_title: Bonnie Bassler is tapping into bacterial conversations

more: Breathing oxygen means using oxygen to burn food completely, all the way to carbon dioxide and water. Without oxygen, a cell gets only 2 ATP, its energy currency, from each sugar molecule. With oxygen, electrons from that sugar flow down a chain of proteins to oxygen, which pulls on them hard, and the cell makes about 30 to 36 ATP. As physicist Erwin Schrödinger noted in What Is Life?, living cells stay ordered only by continually drawing free energy from their surroundings, and extra energy pays for bigger cells and more computing.
link2_title: Mitochondria, cell energy and ATP synthase

more: Mitochondria are the power plants inside complex cells, and they began as free-living bacteria that were swallowed and kept. Over time they handed most of their genes to the host's nucleus but kept making energy. One cell can hold hundreds or thousands of them, which gives it a huge area of membrane for making ATP. Researchers estimate this gave complex cells thousands of times more energy per gene than bacteria, enough to afford much bigger genomes. Mitochondria still keep their own small DNA, a clue to their past.
link2_title: Mitochondria, cell energy and ATP synthase

more: Complex cells process information with chains of proteins that pass a signal along, each step switching on the next. Such a cascade can turn one molecule touching the surface into thousands of changes inside, and it can combine several inputs before the cell responds. An internal skeleton of protein fibers lets the cell change shape, move cargo and crawl. All of this costs energy, which mitochondria supplied. Yeast cells, for example, use a cascade to sense a mating partner and grow toward it.

A human cell holds about 2 meters of DNA in a nucleus only a few micrometers wide. Complex cells pack it by winding DNA around spools of proteins called histones, forming beads called nucleosomes that fold further into chromatin. Packing also controls access: tightly wound stretches stay silent, while loose ones can be read. This let genomes grow much larger without tangling and let cells switch whole sets of genes on or off. More storage meant room for the instructions to build complex bodies.

Endosymbiosis means one cell living inside another. Long ago, a host cell took in a bacterium but did not digest it, and the two came to depend on each other. The guest supplied energy, the host supplied shelter and raw materials, and over many generations they became one organism. This is how mitochondria began, and the trick happened again later with chloroplasts. Biologist Lynn Margulis championed the idea in the 1960s, and in What Is Life? and What Is Intelligence? Blaise Agüera y Arcas highlights such mergers as the recurring engine of evolution's biggest leaps.
link3_title: It takes teamwork: how endosymbiosis changed life on Earth

more: A chloroplast is a built-in solar panel inside plant and algal cells. It began as a cyanobacterium that a complex cell swallowed and kept, just as mitochondria began earlier. The captured partner brought oxygen-making photosynthesis with it, so its host could now feed itself on sunlight. Chloroplasts still carry their own small ring of DNA and divide in two like bacteria. Land plants, green algae and red algae all trace their chloroplasts back to this one capture.
link2_title: Plant cells, chloroplasts and cell walls
link3_title: It takes teamwork: how endosymbiosis changed life on Earth

more: An eyespot is a patch of light-sensing proteins backed by a layer of pigment, so it can tell which direction light comes from. The single-celled green alga Chlamydomonas has one, an orange spot on the side of the cell. As the cell rolls while swimming, the eyespot turns toward the light and away again, and the changing signal adjusts how its two flagella beat. The cell swims toward moderate light for photosynthesis and away from light that is too strong. It is one of the simplest direction senses.

Sex mixes the genes of two parents. A special cell division called meiosis shuffles each parent's chromosomes and swaps pieces between them, and two such cells later fuse. Shuffling lets helpful mutations that arose in different individuals end up together, and concentrates harmful ones in offspring that do not survive. The oldest fossil evidence for sex is a red seaweed called Bangiomorpha, about 1 billion years old. Meiosis was probably already present in the common ancestor of all complex cells, so sex itself is likely older than this fossil. Scientists still debate exactly why sex is worth its costs.
link2_title: Stages of meiosis and sexual reproduction

more: A many-celled body begins when cells divide but stay stuck together instead of drifting apart. Because the cells are clones with the same genes, they all gain by sharing the work: some can feed, others can anchor or reproduce. Cells signal to their neighbors to decide which job each one takes. One of the oldest known examples is the red seaweed Bangiomorpha, about 1 billion years old, with special cells for holding on to rock. Many-celled life evolved many separate times.
link2_title: The evolution of multicellularity: an update

more: A synapse is the junction where one nerve cell passes a signal to the next. Many of the proteins that build it existed before any animal had nerves. Choanoflagellates, the single-celled closest living relatives of animals, carry versions of many of these proteins even though they have no nerves. Some, such as cadherins, are sticky proteins that help cells attach to things. Evolution often works this way, reusing old parts for new jobs, so when nerves appeared the kit was already in the toolbox.
link2_title: Genome of marine organism tells of animals' one-celled ancestors

more: Fungi grow as mycelium, a web of threads only a few micrometers wide that spreads through mud, soil or rotting matter. Because the threads are connected, food and chemical signals can move across the whole web, so one fungus works as a single network. The oldest possible fungal fossils, from Arctic Canada, are roughly 900 million to 1 billion years old. Choanoflagellates, close relatives of animals, can form rosettes, ball-shaped colonies of joined cells. Fungal networks later helped plants settle on land.

Sponges have no nerves or muscles, yet a freshwater sponge can slowly squeeze its whole body to flush out clogged canals, a bit like a sneeze. The signal spreads from cell to cell as a chemical wave, carried by messengers such as glutamate and nitric oxide, which our own brains still use. One full sneeze takes many minutes, far slower than a nerve impulse. Chemical traces in rocks suggest sponges may date back to around this time, though scientists still debate the evidence.

Before nerves, some simple animals coordinated their bodies with chemical messages and electrical changes across cell membranes. The best living example is Trichoplax, a flat creature 1 to 2 millimeters wide with only a few kinds of cells and no neurons or synapses. Special cells release short protein signals called peptides that change how the whole animal crawls, feeds or rests. Its cells also carry many of the ion channels that let nerves fire. Trichoplax has no fossil record, so placing this stage at this moment is an inference from living animals. It shows how a body can coordinate without a brain.

A body with a front and a back meets the world head first, so it pays to put the senses where the body is going. Biologists call this cephalization: gathering sense organs and nerve cells at the leading end. One of the oldest known two-sided animals, a worm called Ikaria wariootia, lived in South Australia about 555 million years ago and was only 2 to 7 millimeters long. With its sensors in front, an animal could sense what lay ahead first and act second.
link2_title: Ancestor of all animals identified in Australian fossils

more: An axon is the long, thin fiber a neuron uses to send its electrical pulse to other cells. Along a bare axon the pulse has to be rebuilt at every point of the membrane, so it moves only about as fast as a person walks. Making it twice as fast means making the fiber four times wider. Squids took this route: their giant axon, about half a millimeter across, carries escape signals at roughly 20 meters per second. Bare wiring set a hard limit on how quickly a body could react.

A neuron is a cell built to carry messages. It collects signals on short branches, fires an electrical pulse, and passes it to the next cell at a junction called a synapse. Linked into a nerve net, like the one a jellyfish still uses, neurons let a signal cross a body in a fraction of a second instead of the minutes or hours chemicals need to drift there. Neurons do not fossilize, and living relatives suggest the first ones may be somewhat older than this moment. Neurons became the planet's first dedicated processor: cells whose job is to combine inputs and decide what to send next.

A spike is a tiny electrical pulse that lasts about a thousandth of a second. The pattern of which neurons are spiking right now is the animal's working state: what it is sensing, and what it is about to do. Some neurons can keep firing on their own for several seconds, holding a fact after the cause is gone. When a monkey must remember where a light flashed, cells in its frontal cortex keep firing until it can answer. When the firing stops, the memory is lost unless something stores it.

Steering is the simplest useful program: turn toward what is good and away from what is harmful. A two-sided body with senses at the front can compare signals and turn, step by step, up a trail of food smell. The tiny roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans still does this today with only 302 neurons. Branching burrows from the start of the Cambrian show animals probing and turning through the seafloor mud. In A Brief History of Intelligence, Max Bennett calls this approach-or-avoid loop the first of five breakthroughs that built the human brain.

A compound eye is made of many small units, each with its own lens, that each see one small patch of the world. The brain assembles these patches into a mosaic picture. Fossil eyes of the predator Anomalocaris, from South Australia, show at least 16,000 lenses packed into a single eye about 2 to 3 centimeters wide. Many scientists think sharp eyes set off an arms race, as prey evolved armor, speed and hiding to escape hunters that could see them from afar.

A shrimp-like fossil called Fuxianhuia protensa, about 520 million years old from southern China, preserves a brain in three fused parts in front of the gut. Its visual centers are nested in layers, like those of modern insects and crabs, so an image can be processed in stages. That is a big step: one central organ now turns eye signals into decisions. Some scientists question how clearly the fossil shows brain tissue, but later specimens support the finding.

Squid, cuttlefish and octopuses built big brains along a completely different branch of life from fishes and mammals. Instead of gathering almost every neuron in the head, they split the job between huge optic lobes behind the eyes and thick nerve cords inside each arm. In a modern octopus, about three-fifths of its 500 million neurons sit in the eight arms, so each arm can taste, explore and grip on its own while the central brain chooses the overall goal. That layout solves the hard job of steering soft, jointless limbs with endless ways to bend.

Corals and moss animals grow by budding clones that stay joined together by living tissue and a shared nerve net. One polyp's tentacles catch plankton and share the digested food through canals with neighbors in the shade. If a fish bites one edge of a colony, a quick warning wave makes thousands of polyps pull back into their stony cups together. Once a year, whole reefs also time their egg release to the moon and twilight so millions of colonies spawn in the same hour.

Learning from reward means trying something, seeing how it turns out, and doing more of what works. In vertebrate brains, dopamine cells signal surprise: they fire more when an outcome beats expectations, stay steady when it matches, and dip when it falls short. In A Brief History of Intelligence, Max Bennett credits this basal-ganglia dopamine loop in early jawless fishes around 500 million years ago as Breakthrough 2: trial-and-error reinforcement learning within one lifetime.
link3_title: Discovering Dopamine's Role in Reward Prediction Error

more: A synapse is the contact point where one neuron passes signals to the next. When two connected neurons are active together, the synapse between them can grow stronger, and that change can last for days or a lifetime. The sea slug Aplysia learns to pull in its gill harder after a shock because specific synapses strengthen. Scientists at the Salk Institute counted about 26 distinct synapse sizes in rat brains, so each synapse may store roughly 4 to 5 bits.
link2_title: Memory capacity of brain is 10 times more than previously thought

more: A school is a group of fish swimming close together, all facing the same way and turning at once. No fish is in charge: each one follows simple rules, staying near its neighbors, matching their heading, and avoiding collisions. Fish sense neighbors with their eyes and with the lateral line, a row of pressure sensors along each side. Many eyes spot danger sooner, and a swirling crowd confuses predators. No fossil shows the earliest fish schooling, so this is an inference; the oldest fossil of a fish school is about 50 million years old. Herring schools today can hold millions of fish.

Water carries tiny pressure ripples whenever prey twitches or a predator glides nearby. Fishes line their heads and sides with hair-cell canals called the lateral line that feel those ripples even in pitch darkness. Many early fishes also sensed weak electric fields leaking from another animal's muscles and gills. Together, touch-at-a-distance and electric sense fed a map of surrounding space directly into the midbrain.

When a shadow or shock wave hits a fish, waiting to think can be fatal. Most fishes wire two giant command cells, called Mauthner neurons, straight from their ear and lateral line to the muscles down the opposite side of the body. Whichever cell fires first shuts down its twin and bends the fish into a fast C-shaped snap that begins about 5 to 10 milliseconds after the threat. It works like a hardware interrupt in a computer, saving life first while slower brain regions figure out what happened.

Myelin is a fatty wrapping that special helper cells wind around nerve fibers, like insulation on a wire. It leaves small bare gaps, and the electrical pulse jumps from gap to gap instead of crawling along the whole fiber. A frog fiber about 12 micrometers wide with myelin carries signals as fast as a bare squid fiber about 40 times wider. Among animals with backbones, jawed fish were the first with myelin, and it let large bodies and brains react and stay in sync.
link2_title: Myelin: A Specialized Membrane for Cell Communication

more: Plants turn sunlight into sugar, and on land they could reach far more light than algae in the sea. The first small plants probably reached land earlier, but by about 400 million years ago they were spreading across the continents. Fossils from the Rhynie chert in Scotland preserve plants only about 20 centimeters tall. Wood, a stiff tissue that carries water and holds plants upright, let them grow tall. Not long after, the first forests stood, capturing far more of the Sun's energy.
link3_title: Plant life on Earth is much older than we thought

more: Most land plants partner with fungi whose thread-like cells wrap around or enter their roots. The fungi bring water and minerals such as phosphorus, and the plant pays with sugar. The 407-million-year-old Rhynie chert already shows this partnership. One fungus can touch several plants, linking their roots into shared networks: in one forest study, a single Douglas fir was connected to 47 others. How much trees actually share or signal through these networks is still debated.
link2_title: Do trees really 'talk' to each other through underground fungal networks?

more: Water scatters and absorbs light, so even in clear water a fish sees only a short way. Air is far clearer. Fossils show that in the fish ancestors of four-legged animals, eyes nearly tripled in size and moved to the top of the head, like a crocodile's. Peering above the surface, such an animal could see objects about 100 times farther away. The eyes grew before limbs, around 385 to 375 million years ago, so this moment marks the result. Its sense of the world grew from the next few meters to a whole shoreline.
link2_title: Vision, Not Limbs, Led Fish Onto Land 385 Million Years Ago

more: In murky water, a predator appears only a moment before it strikes, so the best a fish can do is react. Seeing far through air gives time to think. Scientists call this the buena vista idea: an animal that spots prey or danger minutes away can compare several possible routes before choosing one. Computer simulations found that planning pays off on land with long sight lines and scattered cover, but helps little in open water. The idea is a hypothesis, not settled. Planning is reacting moved into the future.
link1_title: Why Did Life Move to Land? For the View
link2_title: Vision, Not Limbs, Led Fish Onto Land 385 Million Years Ago

more: Today the air is about 21 percent oxygen. Models of the late Carboniferous suggest it rose, peaking around 300 million years ago, to around 30 percent or more as vast swamp forests released oxygen and buried their carbon. Insects breathe through tiny air tubes, so extra oxygen may have let them grow larger. Meganeura, a dragonfly relative, had wings spanning about 70 centimeters. Scientists still debate how high oxygen really climbed and how much it explains, since some giant insects lived on after levels fell.

Insects fit remarkable memory and navigation into brains smaller than a pinhead. Smell signals from ~50 input bundles fan out onto thousands of cells in twin structures called mushroom bodies, where inhibitory feedback lets only about five percent fire for any one odor. That sparse pattern gives each scent a unique fingerprint that rarely collides with another, making it easy to pair one flower smell with sugar reward. Nearby, a ring of compass neurons tracks which way the insect is heading.

Moving permanently onto dry land exposed reptiles and mammal ancestors to sun, drought and wide territories. Their forebrain grew a three-layered sheet called a pallium, along with a dense cluster called the dorsal ventricular ridge in reptiles and birds. These circuits linked smell, sight and landmark memory to track waterholes, burrows and basking spots. Studies of living lizards show slow-wave and rapid-eye-movement sleep stages that help replay and keep spatial memories.

Amphibians had to return to ponds to lay jelly-coated eggs, tying their minds and bodies to wet shorelines. Early amniotes wrapped the embryo in protective membranes and a breathable shell that let oxygen in while keeping water from drying out. Inside sat a private yolk supply and waste sac, so young could grow larger and wire more complete brains before hatching on dry ground. That portable life-support capsule opened whole inland continents to vertebrates.

After the end-Permian extinction, small mammal ancestors survived alongside reptiles by foraging in burrows and twilight. Inside their snouts, delicate scroll-shaped bones called turbinals warmed each breath and carried vast sheets of smell receptors. Around their muzzles, movable whiskers swept over ground and prey, sending each hair's touch to its own cluster of brain cells. Touch and stereo smell drove the first big expansion of the mammal forebrain.

Most earlier land animals sprawled on four legs, which is stable even with slow reflexes. Early dinosaurs stood upright with their legs tucked straight beneath their hips and ran on two feet. Staying upright at speed took enlarged inner-ear balance canals wired to a fast cerebellum that steadied the head and eyes on every stride. Better balance and fast eyesight helped dinosaurs dominate land ecosystems for 165 million years.

A warm-blooded animal makes its own heat by burning food, so its body stays warm even on a cold night. Nerve signals and chemical reactions run faster in warm tissue, so a warm brain can think and react quickly at any hour. A lizard, by contrast, is sluggish on a cold morning until the Sun warms it. Fossil inner ears suggest mammal ancestors warmed up by 5 to 9 degrees Celsius around 233 million years ago. The cost is huge: much more food every day.
link2_title: Mammal ancestors became warm-blooded in burst of Late Triassic evolution

more: The neocortex is a thin sheet of brain tissue, folded or smooth, built from six stacked layers of neurons. Signals from the senses arrive in the middle layers, deeper layers send commands out, and the upper layers link areas to each other. Every mammal has one, and the same circuit is repeated across the sheet, so a bigger cortex simply adds more processing units. In humans the cerebral cortex holds about 16 billion neurons. It works closely with the hippocampus, which stores new memories.

Deep in the brain, the hippocampus builds a map of where an animal is. Place cells fire only when the animal stands in one particular spot, so a rat exploring a box has one cell for each corner and patch. Nearby grid cells fire in a regular pattern, like the lines on graph paper. Together they keep track of the animal's position, moment by moment, as it moves. Fish, reptiles and birds have similar map-making brain regions, so the ability is probably older than mammals, where it is best studied. Their discovery won the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
link2_title: The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2014: Press release

more: When a rat rests or sleeps after running a maze, its place cells fire again in the same order, many times faster than the real run. Rats even play out shortcuts they have never taken and rehearse routes before moving. Max Bennett calls this neocortical-hippocampal world modeling Breakthrough 3 (Simulating) in A Brief History of Intelligence, while Blaise Agüera y Arcas compares offline replay and dreaming to generative model training.
link2_title: Animals have complex dreams, MIT researcher proves

more: Reptiles hear through one small ear bone, but mammals have three: the hammer, anvil and stirrup. The hammer and anvil started out as bones of the jaw joint in mammal ancestors. Over millions of years they shrank, broke free of the jaw, and formed a tiny lever that passes faint, high-pitched sound into the inner ear. Fossils suggest this happened more than once, in different mammal groups, and much of it later than this moment. In a human embryo, these two bones still grow from the same tissue that builds the jaw. Many mammals hear well above 20,000 vibrations per second.

Flying means steering in three dimensions at speed, using sight, balance and wing control all at once. The cerebellum, a fist-shaped region at the back of the brain, fine-tunes movement and balance, and the pallium handles sight and decisions. CT scans of the skull of Archaeopteryx, about 150 million years old, show a brain of about 1.6 cubic centimeters with large vision areas and balance canals like those of flying birds. Some feathered dinosaurs that could not fly had similar brains.

A flock of 50,000 starlings wheels across the sky faster than any one bird could shout an order. Field cameras show that each bird simply matches speed and turn direction with its six or seven nearest neighbors, no matter how far apart the flock stretches. Because everyone links to seven neighbors, a hawk dive at one edge ripples cleanly across the whole cloud without a leader. Migrating geese and ibises also take turns riding each neighbor's wingtip updraft to save flight energy. Flocking leaves no fossils, so its placement here, as modern bird groups spread after the dinosaurs, is an inference from living birds.
link2_title: How starling flocks move as one

more: In a superorganism, thousands or millions of insects act like one body. Only a queen lays eggs, while sterile workers forage, build, nurse and defend. Ants share news through scent trails, and honeybees dance: the angle of a waggle run shows the direction of food relative to the Sun, and its length tells the distance. A single leafcutter ant colony can hold millions of workers. Ants and termites lived in colonies long before this time, but ants spread widely after the dinosaurs disappeared.

Most fish and insects lay hundreds of eggs and never meet their young, so every generation starts with only what DNA wrote in advance. Warm-blooded mammals and birds invested instead in a few offspring fed with milk or carried food, kept warm, and guarded through a long childhood. Contact calls, scent recognition and bonding hormones tied parent and young into Earth's smallest, tightest communication network. That safe window let young brains stay plastic and copy their parents' foraging skills.

Leaping between thin tree branches and spotting ripe fruit among green leaves rewarded sharp sight. Early primates brought both eyes forward for 3D depth perception, and the line leading to monkeys and apes packed cones into a central pit called a fovea. Three-color vision came later, about 30 to 40 million years ago, in the ancestors of Old World monkeys and apes; howler monkeys evolved their own version. Before signals ever leave the eyeball, five thin layers of retinal neurons filter edges and motion, compressing billions of raw light detections per second by about a hundredfold onto the optic nerve. The eye itself became an edge computer.
link2_title: Evolution of color vision in primates

more: A mammal's neocortex is a sheet about two to four millimeters thick where columns of neurons wire predominantly to neighbors. Early primates still had smooth brains. As monkeys, apes, whales and carnivores grew larger brains, a smooth sheet could no longer fit inside a skull narrow enough for birth and fast movement. Folding the sheet into ridges and grooves packed far more cortical surface area in while keeping short wires short. Over half of a monkey's folded cortex became a hierarchy of visual and social maps.

Echolocation means sending out sounds and listening for the echoes to find things. Toothed whales, such as dolphins and sperm whales, make clicks in their nasal passages, focus them through a fatty lump in the forehead called the melon, and pick up echoes through the lower jaw. Sound travels about 1,500 meters per second in water, so the echo from a fish 15 meters away returns in about one fiftieth of a second. That lets them hunt in dark or murky water.

A bird's pallium is the part of the brain that, like our cortex, handles thinking. Songbirds and parrots pack small neurons tightly, so their brains hold about twice as many neurons as primate brains of the same weight. A macaw's brain is the size of an unshelled walnut, yet it has more forebrain neurons than a macaque monkey's lemon-sized brain. That density helps explain how crows and parrots solve puzzles, use tools and plan.
link2_title: Study gives new meaning to the term 'bird brain'

more: Most mammals are born with fixed calls, but toothed whales, songbirds and parrots evolved brain loops that learn new sounds by listening to elders. Orca and sperm-whale families pass down pod-specific click dialects and hunting tactics across generations, led by post-reproductive grandmothers who remember where salmon run in lean years. Bottlenose dolphins even invent personal signature whistles that work like spoken names over kilometers of murky water. Culture became a survival network in the sea and sky.

Theory of mind is the ability to understand that someone else can know, want or believe something different from you. In a 2016 eye-tracking study, apes looked to where a person would search for a hidden object based on that person's mistaken belief. In A Brief History of Intelligence, Max Bennett names primate prefrontal modeling of other minds Breakthrough 4 (Mentalizing), while Blaise Agüera y Arcas notes convergent social modeling in corvids and whales.
link2_title: Apes Understand That Some Things Are All in Your Head

more: Living in a troop of 50 to 80 monkeys or apes protects against leopards, but it creates a hard social puzzle. Every member has to remember who groomed whom, who outranks whom, and which partners will back them up in a dispute. Vervet monkeys also give distinct alarm calls for eagles, leopards and snakes, sending companions up trees, into bushes or onto hind legs. Social grooming and vocal calls turn a troop into an alliance network bounded by how many relationships one brain can track.

As East African forests thinned into open woodland and savanna, early hominins stood upright on two legs. Walking on two feet uses roughly a quarter less energy than knuckle-walking over long foraging treks, and it lifts the eyes above tall grass. Most importantly, two legs freed the hands from supporting body weight. Hands could now carry food back to family members, wave gestures and eventually strike stone.

On open savannas, elephant families and grazing herds coordinate across huge distances. An elephant matriarch in her fifties remembers rare waterholes from droughts decades earlier and leads nested family units, bond groups and clans of hundreds. Elephants stay in touch over up to ten kilometers using deep 15-hertz rumbles that travel both through the air and as seismic waves felt through the soles of their feet. One elder's long memory shields the whole clan.

Making a sharp stone flake takes a strong grip, a careful eye and a well-aimed blow: one stone used as a hammer to break pieces off another. At Lomekwi in Kenya, scientists found stones shaped this way about 3.3 million years ago, older than any known member of our own genus. With a sharp edge, a hand can cut meat and hide or smash bones for marrow. Nobody yet knows for sure which species made these tools.

A shaped stone holds knowledge: its edge, its scars and the flakes around it show how it was made, so others can copy the method. Unlike a brain, it needs no food or energy to keep that record. The Lomekwi stones from Kenya have lasted about 3.3 million years. Later toolmakers built on this, and by about 1.76 million years ago humans were shaping teardrop handaxes to a planned design. Tools became the first memory stored outside a living body.

Flaking a razor-sharp knife off a cobble is not random smashing: the striker must pick an edge under ninety degrees and hit millimeters from the rim with controlled force. Brain-imaging studies of modern flintknappers show heavy demand on circuits linking hand touch, sharp vision and motor prediction in the parietal and premotor cortex. As early Homo relied on cut meat and cracked marrow, brains grew by half to roughly forty billion neurons. Tools and neural wiring began pulling each other upward.

Cooking breaks down food before it is eaten, so the body gets more energy from it with less chewing and digestion. Some scientists think this let early humans grow smaller guts and teeth and spend the saved energy on bigger brains. Today the human brain uses about a fifth of the body's energy, though it is only about 2 percent of body weight. Clues to fire use at this moment are debated; firm evidence starts about 1 million years ago in South Africa's Wonderwerk Cave, and clear hearths date to about 790,000 years ago in Israel.
link1_title: Control of fire by early humans

more: Shaping a Levallois stone point or hafting a stone tip onto a wooden spear shaft with birch-bark tar cannot be done in one reflex loop. The maker has to picture the finished shape first, prepare a domed stone core in ten ordered strikes, and pause to fix mistakes before the final blow. Brain regions that sequence nested sub-goals for hands overlap closely with those later used to nest words into sentences. Action grammar paved the road for spoken grammar.

Human children take more than a decade to grow an adult brain, far too costly for one mother foraging alone. Middle Pleistocene bands solved this through shared family networks: grandmothers, fathers and siblings helped feed the young while experienced hunters coordinated ambushes of horses and deer. Sharing meat around a hearth rewarded fairness, pointing, eye contact and teaching. Cooperative family bands became the cradle of human culture.

A symbol is a mark that stands for an idea. At Blombos Cave in South Africa, people about 75,000 years ago scratched crisscross patterns into pieces of red ochre, a colored mineral, and pierced dozens of small snail shells to string as beads. The beads may have shown who belonged to which group. Once meaning sits in an object, it can be carried, shown and passed on, even when its maker is not there.

Speech turns thoughts into sound that another brain can decode. A 2019 study compared 17 languages, from Japanese to Vietnamese. Fast talkers, like Japanese speakers, pack less information into each syllable, while slower languages pack more into each one. The two effects balance, so every language studied moved information at about the same rate. The ability to speak is probably older than this moment, perhaps 100,000 years or more. That rate is the bandwidth of the link between two human brains: far slower than nerves, but able to connect separate minds.
link2_title: Similar information rates across languages, despite divergent speech rates

more: Language lets one mind put a plan, a warning or a story into another. Its key trick is nesting: phrases tucked inside phrases, as in 'the man who found the river that floods'. Max Bennett crowns nested language Breakthrough 5 (Speaking) in A Brief History of Intelligence: a bridge that links separate brains into a cumulative cultural ratcheting network. About 7,000 languages are spoken today.

Painting and carving let people store stories, knowledge and counts on surfaces that last. On the Indonesian island of Sulawesi, a painting of a warty pig is at least 45,500 years old, one of the oldest known pictures of an animal, and a 2024 study dated another Sulawesi painting to at least 51,200 years ago. The Lebombo bone from southern Africa, about 43,000 years old, carries a row of cut notches that may be a tally. Aboriginal Australian songlines, sung routes that hold the map of a landscape, show memory kept in song, though their age cannot be dated.

A tribe is a web of small bands, each a few dozen people, joined by one language, shared customs and family ties. Shared words let people trust strangers they had never met, swap partners and tools, and gather for feasts or trade. That stretched the network far past the roughly 150 people one brain can track personally. In surveys of traditional societies, anthropologist Robin Dunbar found tribes usually hold about 500 to 2,500 people.

Farming means planting the seeds you choose and raising the animals you choose, instead of gathering whatever grows wild. In the Fertile Crescent of the Middle East, people tamed wheat, barley, sheep and goats, and farming also began on its own in China, New Guinea and the Americas. A field of grain stores sunlight as food that can be dried and kept for months. That surplus could feed people who did not farm, giving bigger human networks a steady power supply.

Once fields needed tending all year, families stopped moving and built permanent houses of mud brick and stone close together. Hundreds of neighbors now shared walls, grain stores and rituals, so they had to settle disputes and plan work as one community. Around 10,000 years ago, Jericho near the Jordan River already had a stone tower about 8.5 meters tall. A little later, at Çatalhöyük in Turkey, houses were packed so tightly that people walked across the rooftops like streets.

For thousands of years before writing, Near Eastern farmers counted grain measures and sheep with small baked-clay cones, spheres and disks. To stop cheating during transport, temple stewards sealed the tokens inside hollow clay balls called bullae, then pressed each token into the wet outside so anyone could check the total without breaking the seal. Soon accountants realized the outside marks alone did the job, and the loose tokens inside were no longer needed. Three-dimensional counters had turned into two-dimensional signs.
link2_site: Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures

more: Cuneiform is writing made by pressing a cut reed into wet clay, leaving small wedge-shaped marks. It grew out of clay tokens used to count goods, and the oldest tablets, from the city of Uruk in today's Iraq, are mostly lists of grain, beer, animals and workers. Clay does not rot, so memory could now sit outside any brain for thousands of years. Museums hold an estimated half a million tablets, about 130,000 of them in the British Museum.

A city-state is one city plus its surrounding farmland, run as its own small country with temples, rulers and soldiers. Southern Iraq, then called Sumer, held a dozen or so rival city-states such as Uruk, Ur and Lagash. At its peak around 3100 BCE, Uruk may have had up to 50,000 residents, making it the largest city on Earth. Scribes tracked rations, taxes and debts on clay, so thousands of strangers could share work no one could organize from memory alone.

An alphabet uses one simple sign for each sound, so a couple of dozen letters can spell any word. Older scripts such as cuneiform needed hundreds of signs and years of training, so far more people could now learn to read and write. Scientists trace the first letters to Semitic-speaking workers in Egypt and Sinai who borrowed pictures from hieroglyphs. The first letters date to about 1900 to 1800 BCE. Phoenician traders later spread a 22-letter version, standard by about 1050 BCE, around the Mediterranean, and Greek, Latin and English letters all descend from it.

Most people speak and reason correctly without knowing the rules they follow. Around 500 BCE in India, Panini compressed all of spoken Sanskrit into nearly 4,000 short, ordered rules with helper symbols and recursion, much like a modern computer grammar. Around the same centuries, Greek geometers demanded step-by-step proofs from stated starting assumptions. Writing down the rules of valid thought meant anyone could check an argument for bugs.

Barter works inside a village where neighbors remember favors, but it breaks down across busy ports of strangers. Stamped gold, silver and bronze coins of guaranteed weight put a single shared number on food, labor and ships. Prices began carrying compressed news about harvests and shortages across whole seas without any central planner knowing every farm. Markets joined empires and temples as a third way to coordinate millions of people.

The Antikythera mechanism is a shoebox-sized bronze machine found in 1901 in an ancient shipwreck off a small Greek island. Turning a hand crank spun more than 30 interlocking gears, and pointers on its dials showed the Sun and Moon in the sky, the Moon's phase and coming eclipses. Its gear ratios encode sky cycles, such as the 223-month eclipse cycle, that Babylonian astronomers worked out from centuries of records. It was probably built in the 2nd century BCE and is the oldest known geared calculator.
link2_title: A Classical Wonder: The Antikythera Mechanism

more: An empire joins many peoples and cities under one ruler, held together by roads, armies, laws, taxes and written orders. Over the following centuries, Rome in the west and Han China in the east each grew to rule tens of millions of people who would never meet. A Han census in the year 2 counted 57,671,400 people. Couriers on long roads carried written commands across thousands of kilometers, so one decision in the capital could steer millions.
link1_title: Comparative studies of the Roman and Han empires

more: A codex is a stack of sheets folded and sewn along one edge, the same shape as every book today. A scroll had to be rolled through from the start, but a codex lets a reader flip straight to any page and use both sides of every sheet. Romans first described codices in the 1st century, and by about the year 300 they were as common as scrolls. Jumping to any page made stored knowledge much faster to search.

Multiplying large numbers in Roman numerals is slow enough that merchants needed counting boards or pebbles. Hindu-Arabic numerals gave each column ten times the value of the one to its right and used a symbol for zero to mark an empty column. Writing in ninth-century Baghdad, Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi explained step-by-step pen-and-paper recipes for arithmetic and algebra; our word algorithm comes from his name. Calculation moved out of the head and onto paper.

Papyrus rotted in damp climates and parchment needed whole flocks of sheep skins for one big bible. Papermaking, invented earlier in China from mulberry bark and hemp rags, reached Samarkand and eighth-century Baghdad, where waterwheels pounded linen rags into cheap, smooth sheets. Bookshops and public libraries multiplied from Cairo to Córdoba centuries before European movable type. When printing presses later arrived, rag paper was the cheap medium waiting to feed them.
link2_title: Paper in the medieval Islamic world

more: A printing press pushes inked metal letters onto paper, so one page of set type can make hundreds of identical copies. Around 1450 in Mainz, Germany, Johannes Gutenberg combined reusable metal type, oil-based ink and a screw press, building on movable type first invented in China and Korea. By 1500, presses in about 270 European cities had printed more than 20 million copies. With so many copies, knowledge spread quickly and was far harder to lose.

A mechanical calculator does arithmetic with gears: you turn dials, and the wheels carry each 10 over to the next column by themselves. In 1642 a teenage Blaise Pascal built one to help his father, a tax official, add up money. In the 1670s Gottfried Leibniz designed a stepped drum so his machine could also multiply and divide. For the first time a machine, not a mind, did the computing, and Leibniz later described binary, counting with only 0 and 1.

A scientific journal is a regular publication where researchers report what they found and how, so others can check it. The Royal Society's Philosophical Transactions began in London on 6 March 1665 and is still published today. Printed copies meant a discovery made in one city could be tested in many others. Over the next two centuries this grew into peer review, where experts check a paper before it appears, so mistakes get caught and shared knowledge corrects itself.
link1_title: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society

more: A steam engine burns fuel to boil water, and the expanding steam pushes a piston that turns wheels, pumps and looms. Coal is the remains of ancient plants, sunlight stored for hundreds of millions of years: one kilogram releases about 24 megajoules, roughly what a person eats in three days. By the 1840s steam railways, ships and factories were spreading out from Britain. Even so, world energy use was still mostly wood, about 0.85 terawatts in all, and coal gave only about a twentieth. For the first time machines tapped a power supply far bigger than muscles, wind or water could give.

The electrical telegraph sends messages as pulses of electric current along a wire, coded as the dots and dashes of Morse code. On 24 May 1844, Samuel Morse sent "What hath God wrought" from Washington to Baltimore, about 60 kilometers away, almost instantly. By 1861 a line crossed the United States and put the Pony Express out of business. News, prices and orders that once took weeks now arrived in minutes, so distant people could act together.

Herman Hollerith's tabulating machine read facts about each person from holes punched in a card. When a metal pin passed through a hole into a cup of mercury, it closed an electric circuit and moved a counting dial forward by one. The 1880 census had taken eight years to process by hand, but the 1890 count, using about 60 million cards, finished months ahead of schedule. Hollerith's company later became part of IBM.
link2_title: Making Sense of the Census: Hollerith's Punched Card Solution

more: An electronic computer does arithmetic with switches that have no moving parts, so they flip thousands of times faster than gears. ENIAC, finished in 1945 at the University of Pennsylvania, used about 18,000 vacuum tubes, weighed some 27 tonnes and could do 5,000 additions per second. It was built to calculate artillery tables for the US Army. That same year, John von Neumann's report on its successor, EDVAC, described how to keep a program in memory.

A stored-program computer keeps its instructions in the same memory as its data, as numbers it can read, copy and even change. ENIAC had to be rewired by hand with cables and switches for each new job, which could take days. With stored programs, switching tasks just means loading new numbers. The idea was written up for EDVAC in 1945, and the Manchester Baby in England ran the first such program on 21 June 1948: 17 instructions, running for 52 minutes.

A microchip, or integrated circuit, builds many transistors and the wires between them on one small slice of silicon. Jack Kilby showed the first one in 1958, and Robert Noyce soon found a flat design that factories could print in large numbers. In 1965 Gordon Moore noticed that the number of parts per chip was doubling about every year, a trend later called Moore's law. Intel's first microprocessor, in 1971, held about 2,300 transistors; today's largest chips hold over 100 billion.
link2_title: Moore's Law Predicts the Future of Integrated Circuits
link3_title: Practical Monolithic Integrated Circuit Concept Patented

more: Working memory holds the numbers a running program is using right now. Early computers threaded tiny magnetic rings, called cores, onto wire grids, one ring per bit. In 1966 Robert Dennard at IBM realized a bit could be stored as electric charge on a tiny capacitor guarded by one transistor. The charge leaks away, so the chip must refresh it many times a second, which is why it is called dynamic. Intel's 1103 of 1970, holding 1,024 bits, was the first DRAM chip sold.
link3_title: MOS Dynamic RAM Competes with Magnetic Core Memory on Price

more: ARPANET was a US research network that let distant computers share work by sending messages chopped into small packets. Each packet can travel its own route, so the network keeps working if one line fails. Planning began in 1966, and on 29 October 1969 a student at UCLA tried to log in to a computer at SRI in northern California. The system crashed after two letters, "LO", but the next try worked, and today's internet grew from there.

An optical fiber is a glass thread about as thin as a hair that carries pulses of laser light. The light stays trapped inside because it keeps reflecting off the edge of the glass, even around gentle bends, and it travels at about 200,000 kilometers per second. In 1966 Charles Kao showed that purer glass could carry light for kilometers, work that won a Nobel Prize in 2009. The first fiber cable across the Atlantic, TAT-8, opened in 1988.
link2_title: The Nobel Prize in Physics 2009: Popular information

more: Digital storage keeps information as long strings of 0s and 1s on hard drives, discs and memory chips. Unlike paper, film or vinyl, a digital file can be copied perfectly, searched by machine and sent anywhere in seconds. Researchers Martin Hilbert and Priscila López estimated that the world's digital storage capacity overtook all analog storage around the turn of the millennium, in about 2002. By 2007, about 94 percent of humanity's stored information was digital.
link2_title: How Much Information Is There in the World?

more: The World Wide Web is a system of pages joined by links, which anyone with a browser can read over the internet. Tim Berners-Lee invented it in 1989 at CERN, the physics lab near Geneva, and the first website went online in 1991. Because any page can point to any other, knowledge from millions of authors joined into one searchable whole. By 2000 a few hundred million people were online, and the web was becoming humanity's shared library and meeting place.
link2_title: The World Wide Web project (the first website)
link3_title: What's the Difference Between the Internet and the Web?

more: A graphics processing unit, or GPU, was built to color millions of screen pixels at once using hundreds or thousands of small math units working side by side. Training a neural network needs the same kind of huge, repetitive multiplication, so researchers borrowed the chips. In 2012 AlexNet, trained on two gaming GPUs at the University of Toronto, won a major image-recognition contest with a 15.3 percent error rate, more than 10 points ahead of the runner-up.

A transformer is a neural network design that reads a whole passage at once and uses "attention" to work out which words matter most to each other. Google researchers introduced it in 2017, and because it runs well on GPUs it could be scaled up and trained on huge amounts of web text. In 2020 GPT-3, with 175 billion adjustable numbers, showed that predicting the next token at scale could write, translate and code. Researchers such as Max Bennett and Blaise Agüera y Arcas debate whether sequence prediction captures the core of intelligence or still lacks grounded animal world models.

Earth's power budget adds up two engines: the power living cells and animals burn to stay alive, about 65 terawatts in this site's bottom-up count (14 for microbes, 48.5 for plant, fungal and other complex cells, 2.5 for animals), and the machines people run. Measured from the top down, plants and algae store energy as new growth at about 130 terawatts, so the bottom-up count may be low. Human technology now uses about 19.5 terawatts, a terawatt being a trillion watts, and about 80 percent of it still comes from burning coal, oil and gas. Shared out, that is about 2,400 watts for every person alive, some 24 times the roughly 100 watts a human body runs on. Data centers are a small but fast-growing slice.

An AI supercomputer links tens or hundreds of thousands of GPU chips with fast cables so they can train or run one giant model together. In 2024 the company xAI built a cluster of about 100,000 GPUs in Memphis, Tennessee, in just 122 days. At roughly 300 billion billion operations per second, such a cluster does in one second what ENIAC, at 5,000 additions per second, would need nearly 2 billion years to finish.

High Bandwidth Memory, or HBM, stacks thin DRAM chips into a tower and places it right beside an AI processor. Thousands of tiny vertical wires running through the silicon let data move between memory and processor at a few terabytes per second. That matters because an AI model must keep billions of numbers in working memory and fetch them constantly. Nvidia's H100 chip, for example, carries 80 gigabytes of HBM, and each cell's charge must be topped up many times a second.

A reasoning model is an AI language model trained to work through a problem in many written steps, checking and revising, before it gives a final answer. Spending more computing time on each question often buys better answers, much like a student showing their work. OpenAI's o1, released in 2024, was an early example. On a hard US high school math contest, it solved about 74 percent of problems on average, against 12 percent for its earlier model, GPT-4o.

A zettabyte is a 1 followed by 21 zeros of bytes, and one byte can hold a single letter of text. The world's hard drives, flash chips and tapes now hold about 15 of them, roughly 1.8 terabytes for every person alive. Most of it sits in data centers, where drives keep spinning, chips stay powered and data is copied to new hardware every few years before the old wears out. Unlike a clay tablet, this memory lasts only while it gets power and care.

Today's planetary network links people, phones, computers, sensors and data centers into one system. About 6 billion people, almost three in four, now use the internet, according to the UN's telecommunications agency. Undersea fiber cables, about as thick as a garden hose, carry about 99 percent of the data that crosses oceans. A message can reach almost anyone on Earth in under a second, so billions of people can share news, work and ideas almost as one.

Before cells had walls or enzymes, short chains of RNA resting on mineral surfaces could pair letter-for-letter with loose building blocks in warm water. Because one strand guided the order of the next, a useful sequence could leave daughters behind. Copying errors were frequent, roughly one typo every hundred letters, which kept early templates short. Yet even rough template copying crossed a threshold: matter had begun manufacturing copies of its own pattern.

A bacterium is a complete, self-building factory smaller than a speck of dust. Given sugar, salts and water, it copies millions of DNA letters, builds thousands of new ribosomes and membrane parts, and pinches cleanly into two working cells in as little as twenty minutes. Mathematician John von Neumann realized in the 1940s that any true self-reproducing machine needs both a passive instruction tape and a physical constructor that builds the body—a layout every dividing cell already mastered.

Once a host cell swallowed the bacteria that became mitochondria, simply pinching in half was no longer enough. Now two merged partners had to divide in step without losing chromosomes or leaving a daughter cell without power plants. Complex cells solved this with mitosis: protein cables called spindle fibers latch onto each duplicated chromosome and pull one exact set to each side while mitochondria divide inside the cytoplasm.

If a many-celled body grew new offspring by splitting off big chunks, rogue mutant cells could ride along and ruin the teamwork. Most complex plants and animals instead squeeze reproduction through a single fertilized cell—a spore or egg. Starting over from one cell guarantees that every muscle, leaf or nerve cell in the new body shares the exact same genes, so they cooperate while growing from a fresh blueprint.

Fruit flies, fishes and humans build startlingly different bodies using the same ancient family of master-switch genes, called Hox genes. Laid out in head-to-tail order along the chromosome, Hox switches tell each strip of an embryo whether to grow antennae, ribs, fins or legs, guided by chemical and bioelectric tissue gradients. Tweaking when a switch turns on lets evolution manufacture new body shapes without rewriting every part from scratch.

In the ocean, eggs and sperm can simply float into water, but on dry land a naked embryo dries up and dies. Early land plants wrapped tough waterproof coats around microscopic spores, and seed plants later packed a baby plant inside a protective shell alongside its own lunchbox of starch and oil. Carried by wind or animals, a seed can wait months or years before sprouting into a giant tree.

More than four in five insect species—beetles, bees, ants, flies and butterflies—build two completely different bodies from one genome. First hatches a soft caterpillar or grub built purely to eat and grow. Inside a pupa, most larval tissues dissolve into nutrient soup while tiny tucked-away clusters called imaginal discs unfold into compound eyes, wings and legs. Adults and young never compete for the same food.

In an ant, honeybee or termite colony, reproduction moves up a level from the individual insect to the whole nest. One or a few queens lay thousands to millions of eggs, while sterile workers—often fed different larval diets from the very same genes—build tunnels, nurse brood and defend the walls. Just as your skin cells let germline cells handle reproduction, worker castes act as the disposable body of a superorganism.

Growing a large, richly wired brain takes steady warmth and rich fuel long before a youngster can hunt for itself. Placental mammals nourish the embryo directly from the mother's bloodstream before birth and follow it with months or years of nutrient-dense milk; birds achieve a parallel feat by brooding warm eggs and bringing food to the nest. Subsidized growth bought young brains time to wire up by learning.

Animals grow claws and teeth from DNA, which takes thousands of generations to reshape. Early hominins began manufacturing sharp edges outside their bodies by striking flakes off stone cores at controlled angles. A good blade design could now reproduce in minutes whenever a learner watched an experienced knapper's hands—launching manufactured technology long before metal or machines.

For billions of years, natural selection decided which seeds sprouted and which calves grew up. Early farmers stepped into that loop by saving plump, non-shattering grain heads and breeding calmer sheep, cattle and rice varieties. Within a few thousand harvests, human-guided reproduction turned wild grasses into high-yield crops that powered cities and civilizations.

Gutenberg's deepest breakthrough was not the wooden screw press—wine and olive makers already had presses—but his adjustable hand mold. By carving one hard steel punch per letter, stamping it into copper, and pouring molten lead-tin alloy in, a workshop could manufacture thousands of interchangeable metal letters of exact height in hours. Mass-manufactured parts arrived four centuries before assembly lines.

Before 1800, every bolt and gear was filed by hand, so parts from two workshops rarely fit each other. Steam-driven slide-rest lathes, planers and milling machines let metal tools cut metal to fractions of a millimeter. Crucially, machine tools are machines that manufacture other machines—engines, printing presses, telegraphs and looms—multiplying industrial capacity generation after generation.

Nobody solders a hundred billion transistors by hand. Instead, chip fabs coat a mirror-smooth silicon wafer with light-sensitive film and shine ultraviolet light through a patterned mask, shrinking the circuit image onto the silicon like a microscopic photograph. Etching and baking layer upon layer stamps out whole processors in parallel—turning manufacturing back into optical template copying.

Modern frontier chips are printed by extreme ultraviolet scanners whose 13.5-nanometer light is made by blasting falling tin droplets with lasers 50,000 times a second, bounced off mirrors smooth to a single atom. In parallel, benchtop DNA synthesizers now print million-letter bacterial genomes from computer files. Unlike a bacterium, though, a chip fab needs a global web of thousands of factories and engineers to build.

Today AI models help lay out dense wire routes on new AI chips, write and test software, and design novel folded proteins in seconds. That closes part of the loop where thinking machines help design their own successors. Yet unlike a living cell—which builds a full copy of itself from water and sugar—every silicon chip still depends on mines, power grids, cleanrooms and human hands.

When complex cells grew a thousand times larger in volume than bacteria, random drifting became hours too slow to move supplies across the cell. Evolution solved this by turning bacterial division rings into hollow, one-way pipes called microtubules and modifying tiny enzyme switches into two-footed walkers. Powered by ATP from mitochondria, kinesin walks cargo outward toward the cell edge while dynein winches packets back in. The very same pipes and motors later built beating cilia, chromosome-sorting spindles and the supply highways inside every long nerve fiber.

The captured bacteria that became mitochondria and chloroplasts originally carried thousands of their own genes. Over hundreds of millions of years, almost all of those genes migrated into the host cell's central nucleus—roughly 18 percent of a land plant's nuclear genes came from its chloroplast ancestor alone. Yet mitochondria and chloroplasts still keep a tiny local genome right beside their energy membranes so each power unit can adjust key proteins on the spot within minutes.

Around 500 million years ago, early vertebrate ancestors accidentally copied their entire genome twice in succession—an event biologists call the two-round whole-genome duplication. Because one working copy of each gene kept essential housekeeping running, thousands of spare copies were free to mutate into specialized ion channels, synaptic receptors, hormones and skull builders. Lancelets never underwent those doublings; jawed fishes, birds and humans still carry up to four cousin copies of many ancient genes.

Whole-genome doubling did not stop with early vertebrates. Bony fishes doubled their genome a third time around 320 million years ago, and seed plants doubled theirs around 319 million years ago—helping both groups diversify into tens of thousands of species. Plants tolerate extra chromosome sets far more readily than animals, allowing instant hybrid species to form when two parent genomes combine inside a single seed.

Bigger genomes mean bigger cell nuclei, and bigger red blood cells carry oxygen more slowly across their membranes. Fossilized bone-cell spaces show that two-legged theropod dinosaurs began trimming away repetitive junk DNA more than 200 million years ago, long before true birds took wing. Modern birds and bats still keep unusually compact, streamlined genomes that support tiny cells and intense flight metabolism.

Flowering plants burst across the Cretaceous world after repeated genome doublings wired new floral master genes. Instead of trusting the wind with tonnes of wasted pollen, flowers advertised with petals, scent and sugary nectar so bees, beetles and birds delivered pollen straight to another flower of the same species. Angiosperms also invented double fertilization—one sperm fertilizes the egg while a second triggers fast-growing food tissue only when fertilization succeeds, saving vast energy.

Each set of human chromosomes holds about 3.1 billion DNA letters, yet fewer than two percent spell out our ~20,000 proteins—roughly the same protein count as a 1,000-cell roundworm. Nearly half our DNA is ancient jumping genes, while hundreds of thousands of regulatory switches orchestrate when and where brain and body genes turn on. Because humans live in modest populations compared with microbes, each child inherits about 70 brand-new letter changes.

For four billion years, DNA was copied and translated by enzymes, never read aloud into another medium. In 1977 Frederick Sanger's team read the first complete viral genome—5,386 DNA letters—followed by the first free-living bacterium in 1995 and the Human Genome Project between 2001 and 2003. Sequencing turned living heredity into searchable computer files, revealing the shared family tree and ancient gene swaps connecting all life.

Once genomes could be read into computers, scientists learned to write and edit them back into cells. In 2010 researchers chemically synthesized a million-letter bacterial genome and booted up a living cell; in 2012 Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier adapted bacterial CRISPR immunity into a programmable molecular scissors that cuts DNA at a chosen 20-letter address. Researchers have even encoded books and films into synthetic DNA at hundreds of millions of gigabytes per gram.

Today Earth's living cells hold roughly 3.6×10³⁷ bits of DNA—split about evenly between microbes and complex cells since animals and plants arose. Genome size and intelligence parted ways long ago: a tiny fork fern holds 160 billion letters (50 times ours), while a lungfish holds 43 billion. Copying accuracy instead tracks population size: huge populations let natural selection weed out sloppy polymerases, so pond protists like Paramecium make just one mistake in 50 billion letters.

Before sex could shuffle two parents' genes, cells needed a precise dance to cut chromosome numbers in half without losing any gene. Early complex cells built meiosis out of older bacterial DNA-repair proteins: homologous chromosomes line up side by side, intentionally snip and swap matching stretches, and then divide twice so each spore or gamete carries one clean shuffled set. Even lineages once thought asexual carry these core meiotic genes, placing the toolkit near the root of all complex cells.

The earliest sexual cells did not yet have tiny sperm and large eggs; partners looked identical under a microscope, a stage called isogamy. To prevent a cell from fusing with its own twin—or wasting time when food was plentiful—single-celled algae evolved chemical mating types, often labeled plus and minus. When nitrogen runs low, plus and minus cells switch on surface recognition proteins, lock flagella together and fuse into a tough resting zygote.

As bodies grew beyond single cells, a tug-of-war split equal gametes into two opposite specialists—a transition called anisogamy. An embryo needs a large reserve of food and cell machinery to survive its first divisions, while finding a partner rewards making millions of tiny, fast swimmers. Middle-sized gametes lost at both jobs, leaving two universal roles that evolved independently across animals, plants and seaweeds: stripped-down motile sperm and nutrient-rich eggs.

Early ocean animals faced a vast dilution problem: a single egg and sperm released at random in the sea would almost never meet. Corals, sponges, worms and echinoderms solved it by synchronizing entire reefs to spawn within the same hour using moonlight, twilight and water temperature, then guiding sperm across the final millimeters with species-specific chemical perfumes released by the egg.

Releasing eggs and sperm into open water wastes billions of gametes and fails completely in dry air. Around 385 million years ago, armored jawed fishes called antiarch placoderms evolved bony L-shaped claspers for direct side-by-side internal fertilization—the oldest known copulation in vertebrate fossils. Internal fertilization turned reproduction from a broadcast lottery into direct behavioral pairing, making mate choice and later land life possible.

Moving sex onto dry continents forced both plants and vertebrates to invent sealed delivery pipes. Seed plants packaged male nuclei inside weatherproof pollen grains that grow a microscopic tube straight down to the ovule without needing a drop of rain. Early reptiles and synapsids combined internal mating with leathery or mineralized amniotic eggs that hold their own private pond, unlocking inland continents.

Many reptiles and fishes let nest warmth decide whether an egg develops as male or female—a risky bet when climates shift abruptly. Ancestors of therian mammals (~166 million years ago) and birds independently locked sex determination onto dedicated chromosome pairs—XY in mammals and ZW in birds—guaranteeing balanced sex ratios in every climate and creating fast-evolving chromosomal hotspots.

Once animals chose individual mates, brains and senses became courtship arenas. Songbirds learn intricate regional melodies, lyrebirds mimic entire forests, bowerbirds sculpt decorated stages, and humpback whales broadcast evolving songs across ocean basins. As Charles Darwin proposed in 1871, picky mate choice creates a feedback loop where sharper eyes, ears and neural pattern-recognition co-evolve alongside richer signals.

A human newborn's brain is so metabolically hungry that no solitary mother foraging in the wild could easily fund several overlapping children alone. Hominins evolved a rare reproductive package among apes: concealed ovulation, enduring pair bonds reinforced by oxytocin and vasopressin, cooperative childcare across fathers and kin, and long post-menopausal grandmotherhood—pooling calories and teaching across three generations.

Since Louise Brown's birth via in-vitro fertilization in 1978, over ten million children have been conceived in laboratory dishes. Cryopreservation now pauses eggs, sperm and embryos in liquid nitrogen for decades, pre-implantation genetic testing screens embryos for severe chromosomal or single-gene disorders before transfer, and lab studies in mice have even derived fertile eggs from adult skin cells.

Landing on the Moon meant trusting a 32-kilogram computer 384,400 kilometers from home, built from 5,600 early silicon microchips and copper wires woven by hand through magnetic rings for 72 kilobytes of indestructible memory. Seconds before Apollo 11 touched down, a switch left in the wrong position flooded the computer with extra radar pulses.
